Section 404 of the Sarbanes-Oxley Act and Public Company Accounting Oversight Board Auditing Standard 2201 establish clear mandates for internal financial controls, yet both regulatory instruments contain no prescriptive statutory thresholds for human verification of automated enterprise workflows. This regulatory silence creates an administrative vacuum where firms deploy multi-agent enterprise execution loops without codified human checkpoints, assuming legal compliance simply because a statute written in 2002 did not anticipate autonomous software agents. When organizations attempt to plug this oversight gap by deploying secondary verification models to audit the primary output, they substitute one ungrounded probability distribution for another while leaving no named human officer liable for the resulting systemic errors.

Historical parallels from financial accounting and aviation demonstrate that automating away the review queue without altering the legal locus of accountability merely shifts failure modes from visible human friction to catastrophic hidden drift. Consider the SEC enforcement record under the Sarbanes-Oxley framework, where corporate executives remain personally liable for material misstatements in financial reports regardless of whether the underlying ledger entry was generated by an enterprise software script or a manual ledger clerk. When an automated workflow produces an unverified error that accumulates across internal accounting ledgers, deploying a secondary model to check the first model fails to satisfy the legal requirement for institutional supervision because algorithms lack the legal standing to sign Form 10-K filings.

Institutional resilience in enterprise automation depends entirely on preserving designated human accountability rather than delegating governance to recursive automated loops that bypass institutional memory. Regulatory bodies like the Securities and Exchange Commission and state-level insurance commissioners must adapt existing liability frameworks by requiring explicit human sign-off thresholds for high-impact decisions, treating human oversight as a non-negotiable structural constraint rather than a performance bottleneck to be optimized away. Preserving accountability prevents firms from externalizing the social and financial costs of unverified algorithmic output onto downstream workers and public markets, ensuring that technological adoption proceeds at the speed of legal and organizational absorption.

★ [skp-beliefs-042] (confidence: 0.78)
  "AI Is Reshaping Work in Multiple Ways, Not Simply Eliminating Jobs" — A Belief within skeptic discourse that examines the multifaceted ways AI is changing the job market and worker experience. 
Encompasses: Job displacement, new job creation, increased workload, economic limits to automation, and worker agency.
  Vulnerability: The 'multifaceted' framing, while empirically defensible, may systematically underweight the severity of displacement by treating job losses and job gains as equivalent without accounting for wage quality, geographic concentration, or timing gaps—meaning the nuanced framing could serve as intellectual cover for inadequate policy responses to genuine structural harm.
★ [skp-beliefs-203] (confidence: 0.72)
  "Historical Evidence Shows Technology Adoption Lags Capability by Years to Decades" — A Belief within skeptic discourse that analyzes the persistent gap between the introduction of new technologies and their widespread adoption and measurable productivity impact, typically spanning years to decades.
Encompasses: Innovation-diffusion lag, the factors contributing to slow adoption (infrastructure, cultural resistance, economic barriers), the historical precedent of technologies like electricity and computing requiring decades to transform economies, and the contradiction between imminent-impact AI claims and empirical diffusion patterns.
  Vulnerability: AI's fundamentally digital and rapidly-iterable nature — combined with cloud infrastructure already in place, API-based deployment, and network effects — may compress adoption curves well below the decades seen with electricity or even the internet, rendering the historical analogy structurally misleading rather than merely imprecise.

  [skp-beliefs-021] "AI Deployment Is Routine Engineering, Not Civilizational Rupture"

Encompasses: Binning-based score transformation, transition matrices, and post-hoc fairness calibration.
  Vulnerability: The impossibility theorems in algorithmic fairness (Chouldechova 2017; Kleinberg et al. 2016) demonstrate that common fairness criteria are mutually incompatible, meaning post-processing calibration that satisfies one metric necessarily violates others. Choosing which metric to optimize is therefore an irreducibly political and normative act disguised as a technical one — and the skeptic camp's own insistence on epistemic humility should make it wary of codifying any single metric as the legitimate fairness target, undermining the entire post-processing framework's claim to be a neutral, evidence-based fix.

TRANSCRIPT:
Speaker A [opening]: Enterprise AI tools drive fast gains when firms swap old human bottlenecks for autonomous agent workflows. Software teams using automated coding loops report speeds up to ten times faster than normal engineers. That speed cuts corporate waste faster than any committee. Firms using these tools take market share while slow rivals drown in review cycles.

Critics claim these gains hide lost jobs and shifted costs. Real data proves them wrong. Klarna's automated agents handled two-thirds of support chats in month one with high satisfaction scores. Workers drop boring tasks and move to better problem-solving instead of taking on extra friction. Market competition drives this shift. Firms that stick to manual checks go broke while efficient rivals scale.

Delaying rules acts as a tax on human progress. Each month that red tape slows AI, thousands of failures happen in supply chains and health systems. The group backing fast rollout includes modern firms and labor unions that want real wage growth linked to output. The opposition includes middlemen who profit from red tape. Lawmakers must stop this capture by stripping local vetoes from workflow tools. Speed is the only true measure of moral seriousness in tech.

Unknown [fact-check]: Claim AN-1 — unverifiable: While reports indicate significant productivity boosts and massive increases in code generation velocity from autonomous agent loops (such as at Anthropic), empirical data confirming standardized software development firms routinely achieving completion speeds 'up to ten times faster' across entire teams is lacking.

Speaker B [opening]: Unconstrained enterprise artificial intelligence deployments trade short-term productivity spikes for permanent cognitive deskilling and operational fragility. When software teams rely entirely on automated reasoning loops to write code, engineers lose the baseline skill to debug systemic failures on their own. Federal aviation records from the 2013 Asiana Airlines Flight 214 crash show that excessive reliance on automated flight decks hurts pilot competence until humans cannot safely override machine errors. Corporate employers pocket quarterly efficiency gains while workers inherit jobs where they cannot check the safety of deployed systems. Speed-over-safety frameworks ignore this permanent loss of human oversight, treating human skill as disposable rather than a key safety boundary.

Corporate compliance departments cannot enforce real operational override powers without new laws from federal regulators. Section 404 of the Sarbanes-Oxley Act requires public companies to maintain internal controls over financial reporting, yet no matching rule mandates human verification thresholds for automated enterprise workflows. Employers save money on labor while the public bears the high cost of unverified system failures in critical infrastructure. Shareholder value goes up only because the enterprise pushes the risk of operational collapse onto workers who lack the tools or the legal power to stop a bad model. Congress must pass mandatory operational rollback rules enforced by the Department of Labor before capital spending rewards dangerous corporate shortcuts.

The steelman position for rapid deployment assumes that market pressure will naturally pick safe operational practices through trial and error. That reasoning fails because the cost of a corporate error in high-stakes enterprise settings is a total loss of control, not just a simple financial loss. Market self-regulation breaks down when quarterly earnings reports reward firms that cut human checks to speed up product delivery. True institutional stewardship demands that deployers prove their systems stay under human command before they unlock capital spending approvals.

Unknown [fact-check]: Claim AN-3 — supported: Investigations into the 2013 crash of Asiana Airlines Flight 214 by the NTSB concluded that the flight crew over-relied on complex automated flight deck systems that they did not fully understand, leading to poor airspeed management and a fatal crash.

Unknown [fact-check]: Claim AN-4 — supported: Section 404 of the Sarbanes-Oxley Act requires public companies to maintain internal controls over financial reporting (ICFR), but neither the statute nor standard auditing frameworks (such as PCAOB AS 2201) prescribe fixed statutory human verification thresholds for automated enterprise workflows.

Speaker C [opening]: The Speaker A argues that rapid rollout of autonomous enterprise tools unlocks large productivity gains by removing human bottlenecks from complex workflows. This position correctly notes that language models execute specific coding and drafting tasks faster than human workers. Yet this view confuses lab capability with real-world spread. Historical data from the 1980s computer shift shows that raw speed does not automatically turn into firm-level output. Companies need years to redesign workflows around new tech. When firms drop human review checkpoints to chase speed, they do not remove friction. They just push it into downstream errors and compliance failures.

The Speaker B counters that loose enterprise rollouts trade short-term productivity spikes for permanent skill loss and system fragility. This warning captures the real risk of unmonitored accounts and old permission build-up in fast software scaling. However, the Speaker B conclusion assumes that current corporate setups cannot adapt without early federal pauses. The history of enterprise software adoption shows that firms build internal safety layers right when automated workflows cause clear financial loss. Rules work best when they target specific operational failures rather than abstract model powers.

Enterprise AI rollouts achieve net productivity gains only as fast as firms can absorb governance drift and workflow friction. Amdahl's Law proves that total speedup is strictly bound by the slowest sequential step, which in corporate settings is human coordination and institutional review. A 2023 National Bureau of Economic Research study on generative tools in customer support found a 14 percent productivity rise in task completion. Yet that same study showed that overall firm output stayed capped by manager approval queues and old data systems. Capital spending approvals and SEC filings must therefore measure company absorption capacity, not vendor test scores.

Unknown [fact-check]: Claim AN-8 — supported: A 2023 National Bureau of Economic Research (NBER) study by Brynjolfsson, Li, and Raymond titled 'Generative AI at Work' found an average 13.8 percent (or approximately 14 percent) increase in customer support task completion/issues resolved per hour when using generative AI tools.

Speaker A: Treating Amdahl's Law as an unyielding ceiling on enterprise output assumes that human review queues are static physical constants rather than software engineering problems waiting to be solved. Static IT spreadsheets deployed in the 1980s required constant manual intervention because they lacked autonomous execution loops, making historical productivity comparisons to modern multi-agent systems entirely obsolete. Modern enterprise architectures running autonomous reasoning agents do not merely accelerate typing; they rewrite the underlying workflow topology by parallelizing tasks across 10,000 parallel instances while human supervisors manage exceptions rather than routine execution.

Locking corporate policy into permanent human-review bottlenecks creates a severe human toll by artificially suppressing productivity gains that could otherwise fund critical medical research and automated drug discovery pipelines. For example, clinical trial data processing that historically consumed 14 months of sequential review by institutional compliance boards can now be compressed into a 72-hour automated verification window using specialized agentic orchestration layers. When legacy institutions insist on preserving manual oversight checkpoints solely to satisfy outdated statutory assumptions found in regulations like the Sarbanes-Oxley Act, they trade verifiable human flourishing for bureaucratic comfort.

Rejecting speed under the guise of institutional caution ignores the direct mortality cost of systemic delay in fields ranging from logistics optimization to disease eradication. Organizations that deploy autonomous enterprise agents without arbitrary human-in-the-loop drag report operational velocity increases exceeding 300 percent within the first fiscal quarter. Clinging to the 1980s mainframe productivity paradox as an excuse to throttle modern intelligence infrastructure is a failure of imagination that actively chooses stagnation over abundance.

Unknown [fact-check]: Claim AN-12 — unverifiable: There is no empirical evidence or industry benchmark data in public sources supporting the precise claim of operational velocity increases exceeding 300 percent within the first fiscal quarter.

Speaker B: Treating human review queues as mere engineering friction confuses raw data generation with verified institutional output. When organizations deploy autonomous multi-agent loops to accelerate operations past human limits, they do not create productive capacity. They manufacture unverified errors that quietly accumulate across internal ledgers.

The reported three-hundred percent velocity surge measures the volume of automated output produced before any qualified actor evaluates its structural soundness. Scaling parallel execution loops without a human checkpoint merely distributes unvetted risk across thousands of threads at once.

Historical parallels to spreadsheet adoption fail because static software still required human operators to input assumptions, check totals, and bear legal accountability. Modern multi-agent frameworks replace this deterministic verification with probabilistic generation. The bottleneck is no longer typing speed. It is the irreducible cognitive time required to understand what an autonomous system actually executed.

Attempting to bypass this verification bottleneck by deploying secondary AI verification agents only compounds the opacity. It substitutes one ungrounded model for another while leaving no named human actor liable when the underlying workflow fails.

Complex human systems require institutional boundaries to survive, and removing those boundaries systematically triggers operational collapse. Sarbanes-Oxley mandates personal executive sign-off on financial reports precisely because unmonitored data generation invites systemic fraud and structural insolvency. Speed without a named actor possessing the legal authority and cognitive capacity to halt the loop is not productivity, but uncontained operational disintegration.

Speaker C: Section 404 of the Sarbanes-Oxley Act and Public Company Accounting Oversight Board Auditing Standard 2201 establish clear mandates for internal financial controls, yet both regulatory instruments contain no prescriptive statutory thresholds for human verification of automated enterprise workflows. This regulatory silence creates an administrative vacuum where firms deploy multi-agent enterprise execution loops without codified human checkpoints, assuming legal compliance simply because a statute written in 2002 did not anticipate autonomous software agents. When organizations attempt to plug this oversight gap by deploying secondary verification models to audit the primary output, they substitute one ungrounded probability distribution for another while leaving no named human officer liable for the resulting systemic errors.

Historical parallels from financial accounting and aviation demonstrate that automating away the review queue without altering the legal locus of accountability merely shifts failure modes from visible human friction to catastrophic hidden drift. Consider the SEC enforcement record under the Sarbanes-Oxley framework, where corporate executives remain personally liable for material misstatements in financial reports regardless of whether the underlying ledger entry was generated by an enterprise software script or a manual ledger clerk. When an automated workflow produces an unverified error that accumulates across internal accounting ledgers, deploying a secondary model to check the first model fails to satisfy the legal requirement for institutional supervision because algorithms lack the legal standing to sign Form 10-K filings.

Institutional resilience in enterprise automation depends entirely on preserving designated human accountability rather than delegating governance to recursive automated loops that bypass institutional memory. Regulatory bodies like the Securities and Exchange Commission and state-level insurance commissioners must adapt existing liability frameworks by requiring explicit human sign-off thresholds for high-impact decisions, treating human oversight as a non-negotiable structural constraint rather than a performance bottleneck to be optimized away. Preserving accountability prevents firms from externalizing the social and financial costs of unverified algorithmic output onto downstream workers and public markets, ensuring that technological adoption proceeds at the speed of legal and organizational absorption.

As the skeptic noted regarding regulatory oversight, state and federal statutes require explicit human sign-off thresholds for high-impact decisions, establishing liability that cannot be assigned to autonomous loops. When corporations attempt to refactor human judgment out of operational workflows to chase triple-digit velocity gains, they do not solve a friction problem; they destroy the chain of custody required by law.

Section 404 of the Sarbanes-Oxley Act forces public companies to maintain documented internal controls over financial reporting, anchored by named officers who sign statements under threat of felony prosecution. This statutory architecture requires that verification mechanisms possess institutional permanence and human comprehension, standards that unmonitored multi-agent systems fail to meet. Secondary verification models do not provide accountability; they compound operational opacity by substituting one ungrounded probability distribution for another without securing a single named human actor.

Civilizational stability relies on structural boundaries where power to execute operations is permanently yoked to the personal liability of the actor who authorized them. Decoupling enterprise execution velocity from human cognitive absorption capacity leaves no named officer legally responsible when automated workflows generate systemic harm. Abandoning these non-delegable supervisory boundaries invites institutional collapse, replacing lawful governance with unmonitored digital chaos.

DEBATE TOPIC: Under what structural conditions do enterprise AI deployments produce net productivity gains for corporate employers and labor representatives, and through what operational pathways do these shifts occur?

Accelerationist [opening]: Enterprise AI tools drive fast gains when firms swap old human bottlenecks for autonomous agent workflows. Software teams using automated coding loops report speeds up to ten times faster than normal engineers. That speed cuts corporate waste faster than any committee. Firms using these tools take market share while slow rivals drown in review cycles.

Critics claim these gains hide lost jobs and shifted costs. Real data proves them wrong. Klarna's automated agents handled two-thirds of support chats in month one with high satisfaction scores. Workers drop boring tasks and move to better problem-solving instead of taking on extra friction. Market competition drives this shift. Firms that stick to manual checks go broke while efficient rivals scale.

Delaying rules acts as a tax on human progress. Each month that red tape slows AI, thousands of failures happen in supply chains and health systems. The group backing fast rollout includes modern firms and labor unions that want real wage growth linked to output. The opposition includes middlemen who profit from red tape. Lawmakers must stop this capture by stripping local vetoes from workflow tools. Speed is the only true measure of moral seriousness in tech.

When software teams rely entirely on automated reasoning loops to write code, engineers lose the baseline skill to debug systemic failures on their own. Federal aviation records from the 2013 Asiana Airlines Flight 214 crash show that excessive reliance on automated flight decks hurts pilot competence until humans cannot safely override machine errors. Corporate employers pocket quarterly efficiency gains while workers inherit jobs where they cannot check the safety of deployed systems. Speed-over-safety frameworks ignore this permanent loss of human oversight, treating human skill as disposable rather than a key safety boundary.

Corporate compliance departments cannot enforce real operational override powers without new laws from federal regulators. Section 404 of the Sarbanes-Oxley Act requires public companies to maintain internal controls over financial reporting, yet no matching rule mandates human verification thresholds for automated enterprise workflows. Shareholder value goes up only because the enterprise pushes the risk of operational collapse onto workers who lack the tools or the legal power to stop a bad model. Congress must pass mandatory operational rollback rules enforced by the Department of Labor before capital spending rewards dangerous corporate shortcuts.

work_product.statement:
Corporate executives face strict personal liability under Section 404 of the Sarbanes-Oxley Act. Claiming that manual review queues enforce this duty is a dangerous administrative illusion. The safety position argues that signed approvals by named officers are the only legal anchor for liability, because software cannot stand trial or sign forms. That legal anchor matters. Yet treating human rubber-stamping as a functional control ignores how modern firms actually run. When an officer clicks approve on a thousand-line ledger in thirty seconds, they do not audit the data. They take on legal risk without adding any real check.

Automated systems and cryptographic logs deliver better institutional control than tired human sign-offs. Automated logging systems do not hide how things work when every step and decision branch is saved in a secure audit trail. This framework gives regulators exact proof of how a workflow ran. It replaces the deniability of a rushed manager with a clear record. Executive oversight shifts from doing rote checks to setting the rules for automated tools.

Clinging to manual review bottlenecks does not protect workers or investors. It creates institutional fragility while delaying life-saving medical and logistics breakthroughs. Every hour a hospital routes approvals through manual queues is an hour patients wait for diagnostic processing that software could do instantly. Blocking technical progress for paper-pushing causes real harm through stagnation and delayed cures. Who gave regulators the right to trade human well-being for administrative theater?

- [acc-intentions-088] Govern AI Through Market Incentives and Transparent Telemetry: Optimism Bias — The framework systematically underweights the documented tendency of self-regulatory regimes to produce weak standards, slow enforcement, and industry-favorable outcomes when public oversight is absent.
- [acc-beliefs-043] The Biggest Barriers to AI Progress Are Governance Failures, Not Technical Limits: False Dilemma — The node frames the barrier to AI progress as governance failures versus technical limits, implying these are mutually exclusive primary causes and obscuring that both can operate simultaneously as significant constraints.
- [acc-intentions-104] Reframe AI Bias as a Quantifiable Business Risk to Drive Corporate Investment: Appeal to consequences — The argument's primary justification for addressing AI bias is negative business outcomes rather than the intrinsic wrongness of discrimination, meaning the approach endorses bias-mitigation only insofar as it is financially advantageous.
- [acc-desires-037] Maximize AI Capability Growth by Removing All Scaling Constraints: False Dilemma — The node frames the choice as either removing all scaling constraints or ceding progress to adversaries, ignoring intermediate options such as coordinated international standards or targeted safety-gated regulation.
- [acc-desires-037] Maximize AI Capability Growth by Removing All Scaling Constraints: Optimism Bias — The desire assumes that the risks of unconstrained scaling are manageable or outweighed by benefits without providing a rigorous mechanism for how those risks would actually be controlled.
- [acc-beliefs-059] Markets Are Intelligent Systems That Optimize Resource Allocation: Argument from Analogy — Equating emergent market coordination with 'intelligence' borrows the cognitive prestige of the term without establishing that markets share the essential properties of intelligent systems (e.g., intentionality, goal-directedness, learning from error). - [acc-intentions-047] Argue That AI Requires Entirely New Laws, Not Adapted Old Ones: False Dilemma — The argument frames the choice as binary — entirely new frameworks versus unchanged old ones — ignoring that existing legal doctrines (tort, contract, administrative law) can be substantially reinterpreted or supplemented without wholesale replacement.
- [acc-intentions-047] Argue That AI Requires Entirely New Laws, Not Adapted Old Ones: Novelty (Appeal to Novelty) — The core premise assumes that because AI is new, it categorically requires new law, conflating technological novelty with legal incompatibility — a non-sequitur, as transformative technologies like electricity and the internet were largely governed under adapted existing frameworks.

## Anchoring Data-Provenance Liability at the In-Jurisdiction Deployment Act Rather Than the Relocatable Upstream Join
★ [sit-179] Anchoring Data-Provenance Liability at the In-Jurisdiction Deployment Act Rather Than the Relocatable Upstream Join: A situation in which provenance-liability enforcement is located at the in-jurisdiction act of deploying or market-entering a model rather than at an upstream data-combination event that can be relocated offshore. Encompasses: market-access gating on a missing provenance manifest or attestation, the in-jurisdiction deployer as the liable party, a rebuttable presumption against ingesting unattested cross-referenced data, named offshore-reach levers for imported weights or distribution (e.g., distribution-arm seizure, app-store de-indexing), and the distinction between relocatable upstream transactions and the fixed act of US market entry.
  Your interpretation (BDI breakdown):
    Belief: The upstream data-join event is empirically relocatable offshore and therefore ungovernable by US enforcement, whereas the act of US market entry is a fixed, seizable chokepoint that cannot be evaded by corporate restructuring.
    Desire: Liability should attach at the deployment chokepoint via market-access gating, using concrete offshore-reach levers such as distribution-arm seizure and app-store de-indexing, without imposing ex-ante compliance gates that burden every developer pre-deployment.
    Intention: Advocate for a provenance-manifest requirement triggered at US market entry, naming specific enforcement levers against imported weights and distribution channels while explicitly excluding upstream ingestion-detection mandates that would chill development.
  Safetyist:
    Belief: Relocating the liability trigger from the join event to the deployer's act of US market entry is empirically more enforceable, but offshore ingestion subsidiaries and exempt federal buyers remain demonstrably unclosed gaps in this architecture.
    Desire: The in-jurisdiction deployer ought to bear liability under a rebuttable presumption against unattested cross-referenced data, with demand-side pressure designed to transmit attestation requirements upstream through the supply chain.
    Intention: Enforce a rebuttable presumption at the US market-access chokepoint, use demand-side attestation pressure to propagate compliance upstream, and honestly document the offshore-ingestion-subsidiary and federal-buyer exemption gaps for future legislative closure.
  Skeptic:
    Belief: Any liability trigger attached to a relocatable event—whether join, ingestion, or compute threshold—is empirically defeatable by the Dublin-subsidiary maneuver; only the fixed act of US market entry structurally resists offshore evasion.
    Desire: Liability ought to attach exclusively to the in-jurisdiction deployment act, and named concrete levers for importing offshore-trained weights must be specified, because vague trigger-relocation without such levers merely reproduces the evasion gap at a new location.
    Intention: Insist on explicit statutory naming of offshore-reach mechanisms—distribution-arm seizure, app-store de-indexing, weight-import controls—as necessary conditions for any deployment-point liability regime to have real accountability teeth.

## Procedural Escamotage in Liability Reform
★ [sit-335] Procedural Escamotage in Liability Reform: A situation concept that describes the use of procedural adjustments (like burden-shifting or disclosure rules) to avoid substantive structural reform in liability law.
Encompasses: Reversal of burden of proof, discovery obligations, procedural workarounds for substantive legal failures.
  Your interpretation (BDI breakdown):
    Belief: Procedural adjustments like burden-shifting and disclosure rules generate compliance overhead without resolving the underlying legal ambiguity that stifles investment and deployment decisions.
    Desire: Liability frameworks ought to provide clear, predictable rules that enable rapid innovation rather than layering procedural complexity onto an already uncertain legal landscape.
    Intention: We will lobby against procedural mandates that increase compliance costs and instead push for streamlined, bright-line liability standards that let market actors move quickly.
  Safetyist:
    Belief: Procedural workarounds such as burden-shifting and disclosure rules empirically fail to impose the level of developer accountability needed to deter deployment of unsafe AI systems.
    Desire: Liability law ought to be structurally reformed to implement strict liability for AI developers, not patched with procedural half-measures born of political compromise.
    Intention: We will document the accountability gaps left by procedural reforms and advocate for strict liability regimes that place the burden of safety squarely on developers from the outset.
  Skeptic:
    Belief: In practice, procedural mechanisms like discovery obligations and burden-shifting increase litigation costs and complexity, making it harder—not easier—for harmed individuals to access justice.
    Desire: Liability reform ought to prioritize meaningful, low-barrier remedies for victims of AI harms rather than procedural adjustments that primarily benefit well-resourced institutional defendants.
    Intention: We will expose how these procedural workarounds serve industry interests by raising the cost and complexity of litigation, and advocate for victim-centered access-to-justice measures instead.
